findings.claim: “It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night / Like a rich jewel in an Ethiope’s ear.” (also printed as the extract in practice question 2 and in a flashcard)
findings.truth: The line reads “As a rich jewel in an Ethiop’s ear.” No quarto or folio reads “Like”; “Ethiop’s” is the standard modern spelling, and lesson 7 of this unit already uses it.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1513 line 1224: “As a rich jewel in an Ethiop’s ear;” (1.5)

findings.claim: “Juliet plays along, calling his hand ‘the holy palmers’ kiss.’”
findings.truth: Juliet does not call his hand that. She says that touching palms is itself a holy palmers’ kiss: “And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss.”

findings.claim: The lesson quotes “By any other word would smell as sweet”, and knowledge check 3 marks ‘word’ correct with ‘name’ offered as a wrong answer.
findings.truth: The supplied primary text reads “By any other name would smell as sweet”, which is also the form almost every GCSE student learns and the form lesson 7 of this unit already uses. ‘Word’ is the Q2 reading and is defensible, so it must not be marked wrong either: the quotations are aligned to ‘name’ and the ‘word’ option is replaced with a clearly wrong distractor.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1513 line 1586 (2.2); lesson 7 knowledge check 4 already uses ‘name’

findings.claim: “Act 4 shows Juliet completely isolated. Her father, mother, and Nurse all fail her.” Knowledge check 5 asks students to match “how they fail Juliet in Act 4”.
findings.truth: All three failures happen in Act 3 Scene 5: Capulet’s ‘hang, beg, starve, die’ threat, Lady Capulet’s ‘I have done with thee’, and the Nurse’s advice to marry Paris. Juliet is isolated by Act 4; she is not made isolated in it.

findings.claim: “Friar John is delayed by a plague quarantine in Mantua.”
findings.truth: Friar John never leaves Verona. The town searchers seal up the house he is visiting ‘here in this city’, ‘so that my speed to Mantua there was stay’d’.

findings.claim: “What two-word judgement does the Prince deliver at the play’s end?” with the answer “All are punish’d.”
findings.truth: ‘All are punish’d’ is three words. The same lesson’s knowledge check 4 already calls it a three-word sentence.

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 6: “‘More woe’ is an understatement that emphasises the depth of loss.”
findings.truth: ‘Never was a story of more woe’ is a superlative claim, not an understatement. A student copying this would misuse the term.

findings.claim: “Romeo offers to ‘no longer be a Montague’ and Juliet declares ‘deny thy father and refuse thy name.’”
findings.truth: Misattributed. ‘I’ll no longer be a Capulet’ is Juliet’s line, not Romeo’s, and no line reads ‘no longer be a Montague’. Romeo’s equivalent promise is ‘Henceforth I never will be Romeo.’

findings.claim: “She begins as a dutiful 13-year-old who has ‘not dreamed of marriage’”.
findings.truth: Not a line in the play. Juliet says ‘It is an honour that I dream not of.’

findings.claim: “Juliet’s death is more considered — she tries the dagger first” (repeated in flashcard 13).
findings.truth: Wrong order. Juliet first kisses Romeo hoping poison still hangs on his lips; only when the watch approaches does she use his dagger.

findings.claim: Inline glossary definition: dramatic irony = “Hints or clues about what will happen later in the story.”
findings.truth: That is foreshadowing. Dramatic irony is the audience knowing something the characters do not — the definition used everywhere else in this unit.
findings.evidence: Lessons 1, 4 and 10 glossary_terms of this unit

findings.claim: Inline glossary definition: stichomythia = “A conversation between two or more characters, often in alternating lines.”
findings.truth: That defines dialogue. Stichomythia is a rapid exchange of single alternating lines — which the lesson’s own sentence says two words later.
findings.evidence: Lesson 10 content_html n15: ‘rapid exchange of single lines’

findings.claim: Knowledge check 1: “What type of love does Romeo’s infatuation with Rosaline represent?” marks ‘Petrarchan love’ correct and ‘Unrequited love’ and ‘Courtly love’ wrong.
findings.truth: Romeo’s love for Rosaline is unrequited — the same lesson’s glossary defines Petrarchan love as suffering ‘from unrequited love’ — and courtly love is the tradition Petrarchan verse belongs to. Two distractors are true. The stem is narrowed so only Petrarchan fits.

findings.claim: Practice question 4 in lessons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 is labelled “30 marks — Essay” but its band ladder tops out at 12 marks (10 in lesson 10).
findings.truth: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A Shakespeare is one question worth 30 marks plus 4 for SPaG, and each lesson already carries a separate, correct ‘30+4 marks — Shakespeare Essay’ item with the AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6 split. The 4th item is a mid-length analysis question, so the label is relabelled to the total its own mark scheme awards. (Alternative correction: rewrite the ladders to AQA’s 30-mark bands — a larger change that also invents band boundaries.)
findings.evidence: AQA 8702 spec section 2, ‘Specification at a glance’ (Paper 1, 64 marks, one Shakespeare question); the 30+4 item in each lesson

findings.claim: Three items labelled “8 marks — Extract Analysis” carry mark schemes worth 6 (lesson 7 q5, lesson 10 q2, lesson 10 q5).
findings.truth: The stated total must match the scheme. Lesson 7 q5 awards 2+2+2; lesson 10 q2 and q5 top out at band 5-6.
findings.evidence: The mark strings on those three items

findings.claim: Tybalt: “this intrusion shall, / Now seeming sweet, convert to bitt’rest gall.”
findings.truth: The supplied Gutenberg text reads ‘convert to bitter gall’. Both readings sit in the textual tradition (Q2 vs F1), so this is an edition difference, not an error. Left as it is.

findings.claim: “Juliet’s age — just 13 years old — was considered marriageable in Shakespeare’s time”.
findings.truth: Legally possible but not typical: most Elizabethan women married in their mid-twenties. The lesson hedges it with ‘her father initially says she’s too young’, so it is not wrong enough to edit, but it is a weak AO3 claim.
findings.evidence: Capulet, 1.2: ‘She hath not seen the change of fourteen years’

findings.claim: “The Nurse’s crude comments and Mercutio’s wit are often delivered as asides.”
findings.truth: Both characters make their jokes in open dialogue on stage; neither is an aside speaker of note. Loose rather than plainly false, so no edit.
findings.evidence: 1.3, 1.4, 2.4 — no aside stage directions for either

summary: Ten lessons checked against Gutenberg #1513 and the AQA 8702 spec. Two HIGH findings: a misattributed name-renunciation quotation in lesson 7 (Juliet's line given to Romeo) and a lesson 3 knowledge check that marks the primary text's own reading wrong. Lessons 1, 4 and 8 carry only the unit-wide practice-label defect (F14); no lesson is entirely clean.
